summary: Defines a MIB module for managing pseudowire operation over MPLS label switching routers, adding the MPLS-specific objects that go beyond the general pseudowire MIB.

eli5.summary: This is the control panel for pretend cables running over MPLS networks, with extra gauges for MPLS routers.

questions: how does a pseudowire map to an mpls tunnel
subtitle: The SNMP management objects that tie a pseudowire to the MPLS tunnel or port that carries it.

tldr.problem: The general pseudowire MIB describes settings common to every pseudowire, but it says nothing about the MPLS tunnels that actually carry the traffic.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5602 defines the PW-MPLS-STD-MIB module, a set of tables that hold MPLS-specific settings, link each pseudowire to its outer tunnel (MPLS-TE, non-TE, or none), and map tunnels back to pseudowires.
tldr.outcome: Operators and management software can configure and inspect pseudowires over MPLS using standard SNMP objects. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 5602 is a Proposed Standard from July 2009, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the general PW MIB in RFC 5601.

sections.title: Where This MIB Fits
sections.content:
RFC 5602 describes a model for managing pseudowire (PW) services that travel over different kinds of MPLS tunnels. The general PW MIB module in RFC 5601 holds the parameters that apply to a PW whatever network carries it and whatever service it emulates. This document adds the objects that tie a PW to an MPLS Packet Switched Network (PSN), and it does so in a way that does not depend on the carried service.

It applies to PWs whose PSN type in the PW-STD-MIB is MPLS. Together, RFC 3811 and RFC 3812 model an MPLS tunnel and its cross-connects. The new module supports three cases: an MPLS-TE outer tunnel, a non-TE outer tunnel (set up by the Label Distribution Protocol, or LDP, or by hand), and a PW label with no outer tunnel at all.

Like other MIB modules, it is written in SMIv2 and is normally reached through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP).
sections.eli5: There is already a general control panel for pretend cables. This one adds the extra switches you need when the pretend cable rides through an MPLS tunnel.

sections.title: Three Layers of MIB Modules
sections.content:
The MIB structure for a PW service has three layers that work together, following the PWE3 architecture in RFC 3985. The layering is meant to isolate PW services from the PSN underneath, while still letting any supported service connect to any supported PSN.

  • The service layer holds service-specific modules. They glue standard MIB modules for the native service to the PWE3 modules.
  • The PW layer is the PW MIB of RFC 5601. It configures general parameters common to all emulated services and PSNs.
  • The PSN layer has one module per type of PSN. It associates the PW with the tunnels that carry it. RFC 5602 is the module for MPLS.

Some of the object types used come from RFC 5542.
sections.eli5: It is like a stack of three trays. The top tray is about the kind of cable you are pretending to have, the middle tray holds settings every pretend cable has, and the bottom tray is about the road it travels on.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
The module is designed to meet a short feature checklist. It supports both manually configured and signaled PWs, and point-to-point PW connections. It works with any emulated service.

It also supports three kinds of outer tunnel: an MPLS-TE tunnel, a non-TE MPLS tunnel (signaled by LDP or set up manually), and no outer tunnel, where the PW label is the only label in the MPLS stack. The last case suits manual configuration of a PW over a single hop. For signaled PWs there is always a tunnel in the model, even across one hop, because the packet may simply lack the tunnel label when penultimate hop popping (PHP) is used.
sections.eli5: The goal is one control panel that works whether the cable goes through a special-delivery tunnel, an ordinary tunnel, or just a short direct hop.

sections.title: How the Tables Are Used
sections.content:
A PW row first exists in the pwTable of RFC 5601. If its PSN type is MPLS, the agent creates a row in this module's pwMplsTable, which holds MPLS-specific settings such as EXP bits handling and outer tunnel configuration.

The operator then links the PW to its MPLS tunnel through pwMplsOutboundTable. This is required for MPLS-TE tunnels and for manually configured PWs. For an LDP outer tunnel no manual step is needed, because there is only a single tunnel toward the peer. The agent also fills mapping tables so information can be found quickly by tunnel index.

Only the edge LSR that provides the PW function is configured. Tunnels are unidirectional, so a pair of tunnels MUST exist, one inbound and one outbound. A PW can be tied to one MPLS-TE tunnel at a time, and that tunnel can have several instances (LSPs). Choosing the active LSP is outside the module, but the active one is reported. A combination of MPLS-TE and LDP outer tunnels for the same PW is allowed, and pwMplsOutboundTunnelTypeInUse says which is carrying traffic. Inbound mapping from the remote PE is not configured or reported, because the local PE does not know it.
sections.eli5: First the general panel says a cable exists. Then this panel records which tunnel it rides in, and it also shows which tunnel is being used right now if there are two choices.

sections.title: The Tables and Objects
sections.content:
The module is PW-MPLS-STD-MIB, rooted at pwMplsStdMIB with the identifier { mib-2 181 }. It has five tables.

  • pwMplsTable holds per-PW MPLS settings: pwMplsMplsType (bits mplsTe, mplsNonTe, pwOnly), pwMplsExpBitsMode, pwMplsExpBits (0 to 7), pwMplsTtl (0 to 255, default 2), the local and peer LDP identifiers, and a storage type.
  • pwMplsOutboundTable configures and reports the outer tunnel: a cross-connect index for non-TE tunnels, tunnel index, instance and LSR identifiers for MPLS-TE, an interface index for PW-label-only, and the tunnel type in use.
  • pwMplsInboundTable reports, for each signaled PW, the cross-connect index related to its signaling in the inbound direction.
  • pwMplsNonTeMappingTable and pwMplsTeMappingTable map tunnels or interfaces back to PWs, so an application can quickly list the PWs on a given tunnel.

The pwMplsMplsType value pwOnly cannot be combined with mplsNonTe or mplsTe. The EXP-bits mode is outerTunnel by default, because with an outer tunnel the PW label is not visible to intermediate nodes. Without an outer tunnel, specifiedValue SHOULD be used.

Manual entries in pwMplsTable SHOULD be preserved after a reboot. If a row is found inconsistent after reboot, the PW operational status MUST be declared down.
sections.eli5: Think of five lists. One holds each cable's tunnel settings, one says which tunnel carries it, one covers incoming traffic, and two let you look things up backwards, from tunnel to cable.

sections.title: Compliance Rules
sections.content:
The module defines two compliance statements: full compliance for agents that can be both monitored and configured, and read-only compliance for agents that can only be monitored. Both require the main object groups for the PW table, outbound association, inbound presentation and mapping.

The MPLS-TE group MUST be supported if the implementation lets MPLS-TE tunnels carry PW traffic. The inbound group MUST be supported if PW signaling through LDP is used. Support for pwOnly is not required, but at least one of mplsTe or mplsNonTe MUST be supported if PW signaling is supported. Support for specifiedValue and serviceDependant EXP-bits modes is optional.
sections.eli5: The rules say which gauges every device must have and which are optional extras, with one rule set for devices you can change and another for look-only devices.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is useful for monitoring PW-capable provider edge devices, but it can also configure objects, and anything configurable can be misconfigured with potentially disastrous results. Read-write and read-create objects may be sensitive. Unauthorized access to pwMplsTable, pwMplsNonTeMappingTable and pwMplsTeMappingTable could disrupt traffic. Read access may also reveal how PWs map onto MPLS, so the tables, including pwMplsOutboundTable, may need protection from reading too.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. SNMPv3 VACM and USM MUST be used with any v3 agent that implements this module, implementers are RECOMMENDED to support the SNMPv3 cryptographic mechanisms, and deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. It is the operator's responsibility to give access only to principals with legitimate rights.
sections.eli5: Because this panel can change how traffic flows, only trusted people should get the keys. The RFC says to use the newer, safer version of SNMP.
